units.text: Ninety-six years of football's greatest tournament — every edition, every champion, the road to 2026.

The FIFA World Cup began in 1930, when Uruguay hosted and won the inaugural tournament, defeating neighbouring Argentina 4–2 in the final at Montevideo to become football's first world champions. That first edition gathered just thirteen teams, several of them invited, and the long transatlantic voyage kept many European sides at home. From those modest origins the competition grew into the most widely watched sporting event on earth, contested every four years apart from a gap in 1942 and 1946 owing to the Second World War.

The tournament's format evolved across distinct eras. Through much of the twentieth century the finals settled into a sixteen-team structure, the standard from 1934 onward and used consistently from 1954 until 1978. As the global game spread, the field expanded: to twenty-four teams in 1982, then to thirty-two in 1998, a size that endured for seven editions. The 2026 edition, co-hosted by Canada, Mexico and the United States, expands the finals to forty-eight teams — the largest in the competition's history and the first hosted by three nations together.

Hosting has rotated across continents, reflecting football's deepening reach. The early World Cups alternated between South America and Europe, the two heartlands of the sport. The tournament reached new ground in the twenty-first century, with the 2002 finals co-hosted by South Korea and Japan as the first held in Asia, and the 2010 finals in South Africa as the first staged on the African continent. Mexico, which hosted in 1970 and 1986, becomes the first country to host or co-host the men's finals three times in 2026.

A handful of powerhouse nations have defined the competition's honours. Brazil leads with five titles, the only side to have appeared at every finals. Germany and Italy have each lifted the trophy four times, and Argentina three, most recently as champions in 2022. France and Uruguay have won twice apiece, while England and Spain have each claimed a single title. In all, eight nations have been crowned world champions across the tournament's history — a concentration that underscores how demanding the path to the title has remained even as the field has widened.

Beyond the results, the World Cup occupies a singular place in global culture. It draws audiences in the billions, briefly aligns the calendars of nations across every continent, and turns individual matches into shared reference points that outlast the tournaments themselves. For many countries the finals are a rare stage on which a small footballing nation can stand level with the established giants, and for the host cities they bring a month-long convergence of supporters from around the world. Nearly a century after Montevideo, the World Cup remains both a sporting championship and a recurring moment of collective global attention.

Every edition page draws on cited sources; the result, host and individual awards on each card are taken verbatim from that edition's referenced write-up. A blank field means the cited sources don't state it — never a guess.

The first FIFA World Cup was held in Uruguay from 13 to 30 July 1930, staged largely in the purpose-built Estadio Centenario in Montevideo, constructed for the tournament. Just 13 teams took part: the long sea voyage to South America deterred many European nations, and only four European sides made the trip. There were no qualifying rounds. All 13 invited teams were drawn into four round-robin groups, with each group winner advancing directly to the single-elimination semi-finals, followed by the final. No third-place play-off was staged.

The tournament opened a book of firsts. Lucien Laurent of France scored the first goal in World Cup history, and Bert Patenaude of the United States is credited with the competition's first hat-trick. The knockout rounds produced a striking symmetry: both semi-finals finished 6-1, with Argentina overwhelming the United States and Uruguay defeating Yugoslavia by the same scoreline. The United States, beaten in the last four, were ranked third by FIFA, though no match was played to decide the placing.

That set up a final between the host nation and its neighbour Argentina at the Estadio Centenario in Montevideo, the only World Cup final to date contested between two South American and two Spanish-speaking nations. The occasion carried a curious footnote: refereed by Belgian official John Langenus, the match was reportedly played with a different ball in each half after the two teams could not agree on a single one. Argentina led 2-1 at half-time, but Uruguay responded with three unanswered second-half goals through Cea, Iriarte and Castro to win 4-2, with no extra time required. The crowd is commonly reported at roughly 68,000, though figures vary by source.

Uruguay thus became champions, lifting the first World Cup title and becoming the first host nation to win the tournament, with Argentina as runner-up. Argentina's Guillermo Stabile finished as the competition's top scorer with eight goals. No official best-player award existed in 1930, so that distinction remains unrecorded.

The second FIFA World Cup, staged in Italy from 27 May to 10 June 1934, was the first held in Europe and the first to be shaped by politics as much as by football: the tournament was contested under Benito Mussolini's Fascist regime and used by it for propaganda. Sixteen teams reached the finals, but for the first time the World Cup required qualifying matches, with 32 entrants reduced to 16, and for the first time the host nation itself had to qualify. The reigning champions Uruguay declined to take part, the only occasion on which a defending champion has not competed.

The competition ran as a straight knockout from the round of 16, with no group stage and replays ordered whenever a match remained level after extra time. That rule produced the first replayed match in World Cup history, when Italy's quarter-final against Spain had to be settled the following day. Reported total attendance was about 363,000 across the tournament, an average of roughly 21,000 per match.

Italy reached the final to face Czechoslovakia at the Stadio Nazionale PNF in Rome, before a crowd of about 55,000. Czechoslovakia's Antonin Puc opened the scoring in the 71st minute, but Raimundo Orsi equalised for Italy in the 81st. Level at 1-1 after ninety minutes, the match became the first World Cup final to go to extra time, where Angelo Schiavio struck the winner in the 95th minute for a 2-1 victory. Italy thus became the first host nation to win the World Cup.

Czechoslovakia finished as runners-up, with Germany third and Austria fourth. The tournament's top scorer was Czechoslovakia's Oldrich Nejedly with five goals, a tally that included a hat-trick against Germany in the semi-final. No official best player or Golden Ball award existed for this tournament.

The third FIFA World Cup unfolded across France from 4 to 19 June 1938, the first and only time the tournament was hosted there before 1998, and the last to be staged before war silenced the competition for twelve years. Played amid the rising tensions of pre-war Europe, the event was reduced to 15 teams: 16 had qualified, but Austria withdrew following the German annexation, the Anschluss, leaving Sweden a walkover in the first round. The format was a stark single-elimination knockout from the round of 16, drawn matches settled by extra time and, if still level, a replay, with a third-place play-off for the beaten semi-finalists.

Italy, coached by the formidable Vittorio Pozzo, arrived as defending champions and pressed through the bracket to reach the final at the Stade Olympique de Colombes in Colombes, greater Paris, before a crowd of about 45,000. There they met Hungary. Gino Colaussi and Silvio Piola each struck twice for the Azzurri, while Pal Titkos and Gyorgy Sarosi replied for the Hungarians, and Italy prevailed 4-2 with no extra time required. In doing so they became the first nation ever to successfully defend the World Cup, the only men's team to win back-to-back titles until Brazil matched the feat in 1962.

Brazil took third place, defeating Sweden 4-2 in the play-off at Bordeaux. The tournament's defining individual was Brazil's Leonidas, its brightest star and top scorer with seven goals; an oft-repeated legend that he once played part of a match barefoot remains disputed. No best-player award was presented, as FIFA did not introduce a Golden Ball until 1982.

With the 1942 and 1946 editions cancelled because of the Second World War, this was the final World Cup before a twelve-year gap, and Italy would hold the title for sixteen years, until 1950.

Staged in Brazil from 24 June to 16 July 1950, this was the first World Cup held after the Second World War, the 1942 and 1946 editions having been cancelled. Thirteen teams contested a tournament of singular design: four group stages fed not into a knockout bracket but into a final four-team round-robin pool, making 1950 the only World Cup ever decided by a round-robin final stage rather than a single championship match. It was also the first edition in which the defending champions were eliminated in the first round, as Italy departed early.

The host nation arrived at the final pool in imperious form, thrashing Sweden 7–1 and Spain 6–1 and seeming destined for the title. Brazil needed only a draw in the decisive match against Uruguay to be crowned. On 16 July, at the newly built Estádio do Maracanã in Rio de Janeiro, an official 173,850 spectators packed in for what remains among the highest attendances for any football match; total tournament attendance exceeded one million.

Brazil duly took the lead through Friça early in the second half, but Uruguay refused to fold. Schiaffino equalised in the 66th minute and Ghiggia struck the winner in the 79th, the match settled 2–1 in regular time with no extra time or penalties. The result, met by stunned silence in the Maracanã, became known as the 'Maracanazo' and endures as one of football's greatest upsets.

Uruguay were champions for the second time, twenty years after their triumph in 1930. Brazil finished as runners-up and Sweden took third place. Brazil's Ademir was the tournament's top scorer with nine goals. No official best-player or Golden Ball award existed for this edition, so no individual was so honoured.

The fifth FIFA World Cup was staged in Switzerland from 16 June to 4 July 1954, spread across six host cities in a post-war era poised between amateurism and the early professional game. Sixteen teams were drawn into four groups of four under an unusual format: within each group the two seeded sides played only the two unseeded ones, seeds did not meet each other, and any drawn group match went to extra time. The top two from each group advanced to a straight knockout phase of quarter-finals, semi-finals, a third-place match and the final.

The tournament became the highest-scoring in World Cup history by average, with 140 goals in 26 matches, roughly 5.38 per game. Its most extravagant fixture was the Austria-Switzerland quarter-final, won 7-5 by Austria, whose 12 combined goals remain a record for a single World Cup match. Hungary's celebrated 'Golden Team', the Mighty Magyars, arrived on a long unbeaten run and underlined their favouritism by thrashing West Germany 8-3 when the sides met in the group stage. Hungary's Sandor Kocsis finished as the tournament's top scorer with 11 goals.

The two met again in the final at the Wankdorf Stadium in Bern, before a reported crowd of about 60,000. Ferenc Puskas, recovering from injury, returned to open the scoring after six minutes, and Zoltan Czibor made it 2-0 inside eight. But West Germany struck back swiftly through Max Morlock in the 10th minute and Helmut Rahn in the 18th. With the game level, Rahn settled it in the 84th minute to make it 3-2; a late Puskas 'equaliser' was disallowed for offside in a disputed call. The result, an upset over the heavily favoured Hungarians, became known as the 'Miracle of Bern' and delivered West Germany its first world title. Austria finished third and Uruguay fourth. The 1954 finals were also the first World Cup to be televised. No official best-player award existed for the tournament.

From 8 to 29 June 1958, Sweden became the first Nordic and Scandinavian nation to host the World Cup, welcoming sixteen teams in the amateur-era, pre-television environment of late-1950s European football. The finals spread across twelve Swedish host cities, drawing a reported total attendance of 819,810 across the 35 matches, an average of roughly 23,400 per game. The format opened with four groups of four, each a single round-robin awarding two points for a win and one for a draw, with playoffs to settle ties for qualification, before single-elimination quarter-finals, semi-finals, a third-place match and the final.

The tournament marked the debuts of Wales, Northern Ireland and the Soviet Union, and produced the first goalless draw in World Cup history. Its defining storyline was the emergence of a 17-year-old Pele, who announced himself as a global star and would become the youngest player to score in and win a World Cup final. France's Just Fontaine, meanwhile, scored 13 goals across the edition, a single-tournament record that still stands; he capped it with four goals in France's 6-3 victory over West Germany in the third-place match in Gothenburg, securing third place for his side.

The final, played at the Rasunda Stadium in Solna in greater Stockholm, pitted Brazil against the hosts. Sweden struck first through Nils Liedholm, but Brazil responded to lead 2-1 at half-time and pulled away to win 5-2 with no extra time. Vava and Pele each scored twice and Mario Zagalo added the fifth, with Agne Simonsson netting Sweden's second. The result delivered Brazil their first World Cup title, with Sweden as runners-up, and made Brazil the only non-European side ever to win a World Cup staged in Europe.

The 1962 FIFA World Cup was staged in Chile from 30 May to 17 June, the first and only time the South American nation hosted the tournament. Sixteen teams contested it, drawn into four groups of four; the top two from each group advanced to a single-elimination knockout stage of quarter-finals, semi-finals, a third-place match and the final. It was the first World Cup to use goal average to separate teams level on points, a tiebreaker that helped settle the group standings. The tournament was a notably defensive one: the scoring average fell to 2.78 goals per match, continuing a downward trend, while total attendance reached 893,172 across the competition, an average of about 27,912 per match.

Brazil, the reigning champions from 1958, arrived as favourites but lost their reigning star early when Pelé suffered an injury in the group stage and took no further part. Amarildo stepped in as his replacement. Garrincha became the driving force of Brazil's run, sharing the tournament's top-scorer total of four goals. He is widely regarded as the outstanding player of the competition, carrying the side after Pelé's injury, though no official Golden Ball existed in 1962. The top-scorer mark of four goals was shared by six players: Garrincha and Vavá of Brazil, Leonel Sánchez of Chile, Flórián Albert of Hungary, Valentin Ivanov of the Soviet Union and Dražan Jerković of Yugoslavia.

The final was played on 17 June at the Estadio Nacional in Santiago before 68,679 spectators, with Brazil meeting Czechoslovakia. Masopust opened the scoring for Czechoslovakia, but Brazil replied through Amarildo, Zito and Vavá to win 3–1 and claim a second consecutive title. In doing so Brazil became the second nation to retain the World Cup, after Italy in 1934 and 1938. Czechoslovakia finished as runners-up. The hosts, Chile, took third place by beating Yugoslavia 1–0, with Yugoslavia placed fourth. Among the tournament's enduring storylines was the so-called 'Battle of Santiago', the brutally violent group-stage match between Chile and Italy, which the hosts won 2–0.

The 1966 FIFA World Cup, staged in England from 11 to 30 July, marked the first time the tournament was hosted in an English-speaking country. Sixteen teams contested the competition, divided into four groups of four. Each group was decided by round-robin play, with the top two nations advancing to a single-elimination knockout stage of quarter-finals, semi-finals, a third-place match and the final.

The most arresting newcomer was North Korea, appearing at a World Cup for the first time. They stunned Italy 1-0 in the group stage to reach the quarter-finals, where they raced into a 3-0 lead over Portugal before Eusebio inspired a remarkable 5-3 comeback. Eusebio proved the tournament's standout attacking force, finishing as top scorer with nine goals.

The final at Wembley Stadium in London pitted host England against West Germany before a crowd of 96,924. Helmut Haller and Wolfgang Weber found the net for West Germany, while Geoff Hurst and Martin Peters scored for England, the teams locked at 2-2 after full time. The match turned on a still-contested moment in extra time: Hurst's shot struck the underside of the crossbar and bounced down near the line. Swiss referee Gottfried Dienst awarded the goal after consulting Soviet linesman Tofik Bakhramov, while West Germany disputed whether the ball had fully crossed the line. Hurst completed his hat-trick in the final minute, his three goals at 18', 101' and 120' remaining the only hat-trick ever scored in a men's World Cup final.

England won 4-2 after extra time, claiming their first World Cup title and becoming the first host nation to triumph since Italy in 1934. West Germany finished as runners-up, while Portugal took third place ahead of the fourth-placed Soviet Union. Across the tournament, total attendance reached 1,563,135, averaging roughly 48,848 per match.

The 1970 FIFA World Cup, played from 31 May to 21 June, was the first staged in Mexico and the first held outside Europe or South America. Sixteen teams contested it, drawn into four groups of four for round-robin play, with the top two of each group advancing to a knockout stage of quarter-finals, semi-finals, a third-place play-off, and the final. It was a landmark edition for the watching world: among the first World Cups broadcast in colour and the first transmitted internationally by satellite, with a total attendance of 1,603,975 across the tournament, an average of about 50,124 per match. It was also the first World Cup at which yellow and red cards were used.

Brazil, carrying the pedigree of their 1958 and 1962 titles, swept through the competition, winning all six of their matches on the road to the trophy. Pelé was widely cited as the standout player of the tournament, and the group stage produced one of football's enduring images when England goalkeeper Gordon Banks denied a Pelé header with a save remembered as one of the greatest in the game's history. The knockout rounds delivered another classic: Italy's 4-3 victory over West Germany after extra time in the semi-final, a contest celebrated ever since as the 'Game of the Century.'

The final, at the Estadio Azteca in Mexico City, drew a crowd of 107,412 and pitted Brazil against Italy. Pelé headed Brazil ahead in the 18th minute before Roberto Boninsegna equalised for Italy in the 37th. Brazil pulled clear in the second half through Gérson (66') and Jairzinho (71'), and Carlos Alberto sealed a 4-1 win in the 86th minute with a goal capping a flowing team move that is regarded as one of the World Cup's most iconic. Brazil were champions for a third time, ahead of runners-up Italy and third-placed West Germany, whose Gerd Müller finished as top scorer with ten goals. The third title earned Brazil the right to keep the Jules Rimet Trophy permanently, the first nation to do so.

The tenth FIFA World Cup was staged in West Germany from 13 June to 7 July 1974, gathering sixteen teams in a format unlike the modern knockout. The first round divided the field into four groups of four, with the top two from each advancing to a second round of two further groups of four. There were no knockout semi-finals: the winners of the two second-round groups met in the final, while the runners-up contested the third-place match. The tournament also introduced the current FIFA World Cup Trophy, brought in after Brazil permanently retained the previous Jules Rimet Trophy by winning in 1970.

The early rounds delivered one of the competition's most charged encounters. In a first-round group match in Hamburg, East Germany, making their first World Cup appearance, beat West Germany 1-0 in a politically loaded meeting. It was the only time the two German sides would ever face one another, yet West Germany recovered to advance and ultimately win the tournament. The Netherlands, inspired by Johan Cruyff, captivated audiences with their fluid 'Total Football,' while Poland emerged as a surprise force, propelled by the goals of Grzegorz Lato.

The final, played before 78,200 spectators at Munich's Olympiastadion on 7 July, opened with drama. Johan Neeskens converted a penalty in the second minute to put the Netherlands ahead, the first penalty ever awarded in a World Cup final. Paul Breitner equalised from a penalty of his own in the 25th minute, the second spot-kick of the match and one to each side, before Gerd Muller struck the winner in the 43rd minute. West Germany triumphed 2-1 to claim their second title, twenty years after their first in 1954.

The Netherlands finished as runners-up, while Poland defeated Brazil to take third place. Grzegorz Lato of Poland was the tournament's top scorer with seven goals. No official Golden Ball existed in 1974; FIFA's Best Young Player recognition went to Poland's Wladyslaw Zmuda. Across the matches, total attendance reached 1,865,753, averaging roughly 49,099 per game.

From 1 to 25 June 1978, Argentina hosted the eleventh FIFA World Cup, a tournament played out under the country's military junta and shadowed by allegations of political manipulation and match-fixing. Sixteen teams contested what would prove the last World Cup of that size, before the field expanded to twenty-four in 1982. The format split the entrants into four first-round groups of four; the top two from each advanced to a second group stage of two groups of four, with the two second-round group winners meeting in the final and the runners-up contesting the third-place match.

The host's path to the final turned on a decisive 6-0 win over Peru in the final second-round group, a result that secured Argentina's place in the final and was long surrounded by suspicion of being arranged. Awaiting them at Buenos Aires's Estadio Monumental were the Netherlands, back in the final for a second consecutive time after their 1974 defeat. Before a crowd of 71,483, Mario Kempes opened the scoring in the 38th minute, only for Dick Nanninga to equalise in the 82nd. With the match level at full time, Kempes restored Argentina's lead in the 105th minute and Daniel Bertoni added a third in the 115th, sealing a 3-1 win after extra time.

Argentina were champions for the first time, becoming the fifth nation to win the World Cup as hosts. The Netherlands, runners-up again, declined to attend the post-match ceremonies, citing disputes that included a row over a cast on Rene van de Kerkhof's arm and Argentine stalling tactics. Brazil finished third. Kempes was the tournament's standout figure, its leading scorer with six goals and the man whose two strikes in the final powered the host nation to the title.

Elsewhere the tournament produced a landmark: Tunisia's 3-1 win over Mexico was the first World Cup finals victory by an African team. Across the competition, total attendance reached 1,545,791, an average of about 40,679 per match.

From 13 June to 11 July 1982, Spain hosted the twelfth FIFA World Cup, the first contested by 24 teams after expansion from 16, a widening that opened more places for the African and Asian confederations. The enlarged field made it the largest World Cup to that point, with a total attendance of 2,109,723 across 52 matches, an average of about 40,572 per game. The format paired a first round of six groups of four, from which the top two advanced, with an unusual second group stage of four groups of three; the four group winners reached the semi-finals, followed by a knockout final and third-place match.

The road to the title belonged to Italy, who advanced from the first group stage without a single win, drawing all three matches and progressing on goals scored. The turning point came in the second stage, where the previously goalless Paolo Rossi struck a hat-trick to knock out the favourites Brazil. Rossi went on to top the scoring charts with six goals, won the inaugural Golden Ball as the tournament's best player, and uniquely claimed the World Cup, the top-scorer title and the Golden Ball at the same edition. At 40, Italy captain and goalkeeper Dino Zoff became the oldest player to win the World Cup.

In the final at the Santiago Bernabeu Stadium in Madrid, Italy defeated West Germany 3-1 in full time, with no extra time needed. Rossi opened the scoring in the 57th minute, Marco Tardelli added a second in the 69th and Alessandro Altobelli a third in the 81st, before Paul Breitner pulled one back for West Germany in the 83rd. It was Italy's third world title; West Germany finished runners-up and Poland took third.

The tournament produced enduring storylines. West Germany's semi-final against France finished 3-3 after extra time and was decided by the first penalty shootout in World Cup history, won 5-4; the match is also remembered for Harald Schumacher's violent collision with Patrick Battiston, for which no foul was given. The 'Disgrace of Gijon', West Germany's 1-0 win over Austria that eliminated Algeria, later prompted FIFA to schedule final group matches simultaneously. Hungary's 10-1 defeat of El Salvador remains the largest winning margin in World Cup finals history.

The 1986 FIFA World Cup unfolded across Mexico from 31 May to 29 June, the nation becoming the first to host the tournament twice after previously staging the 1970 edition. Mexico had stepped in when original hosts Colombia withdrew. Twenty-four teams competed, drawn into six groups of four; the top two from each group, together with the four best third-placed sides, advanced to a 16-team knockout phase. This was the first World Cup to use the round of 16 format, followed by quarter-finals, semi-finals, a third-place match, and the final. Matches were contested at high altitude and in heat, several kicking off at noon local time to suit European television audiences. Canada, Denmark, and Iraq all made their tournament debuts. Total attendance reached 2,394,031 across 52 matches, averaging about 46,039 per match.

The tournament belonged to Diego Maradona, who captained and dragged Argentina to the title in what is widely regarded as the greatest individual World Cup campaign. In the quarter-final against England he scored both the 'Hand of God' goal, punched in unseen by officials, and minutes later the 'Goal of the Century', dribbling past several England players from his own half. Across the tournament Maradona scored five goals and provided five assists, a hand in 10 of Argentina's 14 goals, and won the Golden Ball as best player.

France, led by Michel Platini, beat reigning holders Italy 2–0 in the round of 16, then Brazil on penalties (4–3) after a 1–1 draw, before losing to West Germany in the semi-final and taking third place. Belgium reached the semi-finals for the first time, finishing fourth.

The final at the Estadio Azteca in Mexico City on 29 June saw Argentina face West Germany. José Luis Brown opened the scoring in the 23rd minute and Jorge Valdano added a second in the 56th. West Germany equalized through Karl-Heinz Rummenigge (74') and Rudi Völler (81'), but Jorge Burruchaga struck the winner in the 84th minute from a Maradona pass. Argentina prevailed 3–2 in normal time to claim a second world title, after 1978. Gary Lineker of England was the tournament's top scorer with six goals.

From 8 June to 8 July 1990, Italy hosted the FIFA World Cup, gathering 24 teams into a now-familiar shape: six groups of four, with the top two of each group and the four best third-placed teams advancing to a 16-team single-elimination knockout stage running from the round of 16 through the quarter-finals, semi-finals, third-place match and final. It is a tournament remembered as much for its restraint as its drama, recording a then-record-low average of 2.21 goals per match across defensive, low-scoring play. Total attendance reached 2,516,215 over 52 matches, an average of 48,389 per game.

The storylines arrived early. Cameroon opened the tournament by upsetting defending champions Argentina, then went on to become the first African nation to reach a World Cup quarter-final. The host nation, too, found an unlikely hero in Salvatore Schillaci, whose six goals carried Italy to third place and earned him both the Golden Boot as top scorer and the Golden Ball as the tournament's best player. Lothar Matthaus took the Silver Ball and Diego Maradona the Bronze Ball.

The knockout rounds delivered tension over spectacle. England reached the semi-finals before losing to West Germany on penalties, a campaign whose memory in Britain became entwined with Luciano Pavarotti's performance of 'Nessun dorma' associated with the BBC's coverage. Remarkably, all four semi-finalists, West Germany, Argentina, Italy and England, were previous World Cup winners.

The final at Rome's Stadio Olimpico, between West Germany and Argentina, was ill-tempered and became the first World Cup final to feature a sending-off, in fact two, with Argentina's Pedro Monzon and Gustavo Dezotti both dismissed. It was settled in the 85th minute when Andreas Brehme converted a penalty awarded for a foul on Rudi Voller, giving West Germany a 1-0 victory and a third world title. The win made coach Franz Beckenbauer the first person to both captain and manage a World Cup-winning team, and marked the last triumph under the name 'West Germany' before German reunification.

From 17 June to 17 July 1994, the United States hosted the FIFA World Cup for the first time, staging the tournament as part of the sport's major push into the American market. Twenty-four teams contested the finals, drawn into six groups of four. Sixteen advanced to a single-elimination knockout: the six group winners, the six runners-up, and the four best third-placed teams. It was a tournament of firsts on the field as well, the first to award three points for a win in the group stage and the first played under the new back-pass rule, which barred goalkeepers from handling deliberate back-passes from teammates.

The finals delivered records and tragedy in equal measure. Russia's Oleg Salenko scored five goals in a single match against Cameroon, a World Cup record for goals in one game, and finished as joint top scorer with six, shared with Bulgaria's Hristo Stoichkov. Bulgaria, who had never previously won a match at a World Cup finals, reached the semi-finals for the first time. Diego Maradona was expelled from the tournament after failing a drug test following Argentina's group matches. The competition was shadowed by the death of Colombia's Andres Escobar, who scored an own goal in a group-stage loss to the hosts that helped eliminate a highly fancied Colombia, and was shot dead in Medellin days after returning home.

The final brought Brazil and Italy together at the Rose Bowl in Pasadena, California. The match finished 0-0 after extra time, the first World Cup final to be decided by a penalty shootout and the only one to remain scoreless after 120 minutes. Brazil prevailed 3-2 on penalties when Italy's Roberto Baggio sent the decisive kick over the bar. Brazil claimed their fourth title, with Italy runners-up and Sweden third. Romario was named best player, taking the Golden Ball. The tournament also set attendance records, with roughly 3.59 million spectators and an average of about 68,991 per match, marks that stood for decades.

The 1998 FIFA World Cup, staged in France from 10 June to 12 July, marked a turning point in the tournament's scale. For the first time the field expanded from 24 to 32 teams, drawn into eight groups of four. The top two from each group advanced to a single-elimination knockout phase running from the round of 16 through the quarter-finals, semi-finals and final. In all, 64 matches were played across 10 stadiums, drawing a total attendance of 2,785,100 spectators at an average of 43,517 per game. The expanded format opened the door to debutants Croatia, Jamaica, Japan and South Africa, and the tournament introduced the golden goal rule in the knockout stage.

The hosts surged through the knockout rounds, winning every match they played to reach the final at the Stade de France in Saint-Denis, just outside Paris. There they met Brazil, the holders and the tournament's most feared side. The match was shaped before kick-off by an extraordinary subplot: Ronaldo, Brazil's star and the eventual Golden Ball winner as best player, suffered a convulsive fit on the afternoon of the final and was briefly left off the team sheet before being reinstated. He played but was subdued, fuelling a controversy that endures to this day.

France seized the occasion through Zinedine Zidane, who scored twice with first-half headers, in the 27th minute and in first-half stoppage time (45+1'). Emmanuel Petit added a third in stoppage time (90+3') to seal a 3-0 victory in regular time, with no extra time or penalties required. France were champions, Brazil the runners-up.

The triumph made France the seventh nation to win the World Cup and the sixth to lift it on home soil, their first title. Elsewhere, Croatia announced itself emphatically, reaching the semi-finals in its first World Cup as an independent nation and finishing third by beating the fourth-placed Netherlands 2-1 in the third-place match. Croatia's Davor Suker crowned the tournament as its top scorer with six goals, claiming the Golden Boot.

The 2002 FIFA World Cup, staged from 31 May to 30 June, was the first edition held in Asia and the first co-hosted by two nations, South Korea and Japan. Thirty-two teams were drawn into eight groups of four, with the top two from each advancing to a single-elimination knockout stage running through the round of 16, quarter-finals, semi-finals, a third-place play-off and the final. It was the last World Cup to use the golden goal rule, which applied in the knockout rounds. China, Ecuador, Senegal and Slovenia all made their tournament debuts.

The group stage broke the script almost immediately: defending champions France went out without scoring a single goal, losing 1–0 to debutants Senegal, drawing with Uruguay and losing to Denmark. The more enduring story belonged to co-hosts South Korea, who under Guus Hiddink reached the semi-finals—the best-ever finish by an Asian nation and the first time a team from outside UEFA, CONMEBOL and CONCACAF had gone so far. Their run ended in a 1–0 defeat to Germany. In the third-place play-off, Turkey beat South Korea 3–2, a match opened by Hakan Şükür scoring roughly 11 seconds after kick-off, the fastest goal in World Cup history.

The final at the International Stadium Yokohama, before 69,029 spectators on 30 June, paired Germany and Brazil. It was settled in regulation, with no extra time or penalties, as Brazil won 2–0 through two Ronaldo goals (67', 79'). The opener came after Germany goalkeeper Oliver Kahn spilled a Rivaldo shot and Ronaldo struck the rebound. The win gave Brazil a record fifth title; Germany finished runners-up. Ronaldo's brace completed a personal redemption after Brazil's 1998 final defeat, and his eight goals—the tournament's most—were the highest single-tournament tally since Gerd Müller in 1970. Fittingly for an upended World Cup, the Golden Ball for best player went not to a scorer but to Kahn, the first and to date only goalkeeper to win the award, despite his error in the final.

The 2006 FIFA World Cup was staged in Germany from 9 June to 9 July, the first edition hosted by a reunified Germany. Leipzig became the first former East German city to host World Cup matches, one of several firsts that gave the tournament its place in the competition's history. Thirty-two teams were drawn into eight groups of four, with the top two from each group advancing to a single-elimination knockout stage spanning the round of 16, quarter-finals, semi-finals, a third-place play-off and the final. Eight nations made their World Cup debuts, including Ghana, Ivory Coast, Togo, Angola, Ukraine, Czech Republic, Trinidad and Tobago, and Serbia and Montenegro. Fittingly for a tournament bookended by defenders, Philipp Lahm opened the competition and Marco Materazzi would later score its decisive equaliser, the first time both the first and last goals of a World Cup came from defenders.

The final pitted Italy against France at Berlin's Olympiastadion. Zinedine Zidane, who won the Golden Ball as the tournament's best player, opened the scoring from a 7th-minute penalty, chipping a Panenka off the crossbar and in. Materazzi equalised in the 19th minute, heading home an Andrea Pirlo corner. The match finished 1–1 after extra time, but its enduring image came late: Zidane was sent off for headbutting Materazzi in the chest, the final act of his playing career.

The contest went to penalties, where Italy prevailed 5–3. France's David Trezeguet was the only player to miss, his kick striking the crossbar, before Fabio Grosso converted the winner to give Italy a fourth World Cup title. France were runners-up, and hosts Germany took third place, beating Portugal 3–1 in the play-off. Germany's Miroslav Klose claimed the Golden Boot with five goals, the lowest tally to top the scoring charts since 1962. The tournament also saw a record number of yellow and red cards issued. Total attendance reached about 3,359,439 across the 64 matches, averaging roughly 52,491 per game.

The 2010 FIFA World Cup, held in South Africa from 11 June to 11 July, was the first edition of the tournament staged on the African continent. Thirty-two teams competed, divided into eight groups of four; the top two from each group advanced to a single-elimination knockout phase comprising a round of 16, quarter-finals, semi-finals, a third-place play-off and the final.

The group stage delivered early upheaval. Host nation South Africa became the first host ever eliminated at the group stage, while both finalists from 2006, Italy and France, also exited before the knockout rounds. As the field narrowed, Uruguay emerged as a surprise force, reaching the semi-finals and ultimately finishing fourth, with Diego Forlán driving their run.

The final, contested at Soccer City in Johannesburg, pitted Spain against the Netherlands. In a tense, goalless contest that stretched into extra time, Andrés Iniesta settled the match in the 116th minute, sealing a 1–0 victory. The result delivered Spain its first World Cup title and made it the first European nation to win the tournament outside Europe. Germany took third place.

Individual honours were spread across the leading sides. Thomas Müller of Germany won the Golden Boot after four players finished level on five goals—Müller, David Villa of Spain, Wesley Sneijder of the Netherlands and Forlán of Uruguay—with Müller awarded the prize on an assists tiebreaker, having provided three. Forlán claimed the Golden Ball as the tournament's best player, while Spain's Iker Casillas won the Golden Glove as its finest goalkeeper.

The competition drew a total attendance of 3,178,856 spectators across its 64 matches, averaging roughly 49,670 per game. Beyond the trophy itself, the 2010 edition was defined by its firsts: a World Cup on African soil, a European champion crowned beyond Europe, a host undone in the opening round, and a maiden world title for Spain.

The 2014 FIFA World Cup returned the tournament to Brazil, the spiritual home of the game, where 32 teams gathered from 12 June to 13 July 2014. The format paired a group stage of eight groups of four with a single-elimination knockout phase running through the round of 16, quarter-finals, semi-finals, a third-place play-off and the final. Across 64 matches the tournament drew a total attendance of 3,429,873, an average of 53,592 per match.

The competition broke sharply with expectation. Defending champions Spain were eliminated in the group stage, ending the era that had carried them to the previous title. The host nation's campaign collapsed in spectacular fashion: Germany thrashed Brazil 7–1 in the semi-final, one of the most lopsided results in World Cup history, and Brazil went on to finish fourth, behind the third-placed Netherlands.

That result sent Germany into a final against Argentina at the Maracanã Stadium in Rio de Janeiro. The match was settled in extra time, when substitute Mario Götze controlled and volleyed home in the 113th minute to win it 1–0. With that strike he became the first substitute to score the winning goal in a World Cup final. Germany were champions for a fourth time, and in lifting the trophy became the first European team to win a World Cup held in the Americas—the third consecutive title for a European nation after Italy in 2006 and Spain in 2010.

Individual honours were spread across the field. Colombia's James Rodríguez won the Golden Boot as top scorer with six goals, and his volley against Uruguay later took the FIFA Puskás Award for goal of the year; Germany's Thomas Müller finished second in the scoring race with five. Lionel Messi of runners-up Argentina was named best player, claiming the adidas Golden Ball. The tournament also marked two technical firsts for the competition: it was the first World Cup to use goal-line technology and the first to use vanishing spray for free kicks.

The 2018 FIFA World Cup, staged in Russia from 14 June to 15 July, was the first edition held in Russia and the first ever hosted in Eastern Europe. Thirty-two teams were drawn into eight groups of four, with the group stage feeding a single-elimination knockout bracket of the round of 16, quarter-finals, semi-finals, a third-place play-off and the final, 64 matches in all. It was also the first World Cup to deploy the Video Assistant Referee, or VAR, system, marking a technological turning point for the tournament. More than 3 million spectators attended across the 64 matches, an average of roughly 47,000 per game.

The group stage produced an early shock when defending champion Germany was eliminated, its earliest World Cup exit since 1938. The defining story of the knockout rounds belonged to Croatia, the smaller nation reaching its first ever World Cup final on a run anchored by midfielder Luka Modrić. France advanced to meet them at Moscow's Luzhniki Stadium on 15 July.

In the final, France defeated Croatia 4–2 to claim its second World Cup title, after 1998, leaving Croatia as runner-up in its maiden final appearance. Among the French scorers was Kylian Mbappé, who at 19 became the first teenager to score in a World Cup final since Pelé in 1958 and was named Best Young Player. The victory also meant France became the fourth different European nation to extend the continent's run of four consecutive World Cup titles, following the European winners of 2006, 2010 and 2014.

Individual honours were spread widely. England's Harry Kane finished as top scorer with six goals, while Luka Modrić was awarded the Golden Ball as the tournament's best player. In the third-place play-off, Belgium defeated England to secure third place, and Belgium goalkeeper Thibaut Courtois won the Golden Glove.

The 2022 FIFA World Cup, staged in Qatar from 20 November to 18 December, was the first edition held in the Arab world and the Middle East, and the first contested in November and December rather than the traditional May-July window, a shift made to avoid Qatar's summer heat. It was also the last tournament to feature 32 teams before the expansion to 48 in 2026. The 32 nations were drawn into eight groups of four, playing round-robin matches before a single-elimination knockout phase comprising the round of 16, quarter-finals, semi-finals, a third-place play-off, and the final. The tournament set a record for the most goals scored in the 32-team format, with every participating team scoring at least one goal, and drew a total attendance of 3,404,252 across the competition, an average of 53,191 per match.

The group stage produced one of the great upsets when Saudi Arabia stunned eventual champions Argentina 2-1. Argentina recovered from that opening defeat to march on, while Morocco wrote history of its own, defeating Spain and Portugal to become the first African nation to reach a World Cup semi-final, ultimately finishing fourth. Croatia claimed third place.

The final at Lusail Stadium in Lusail pitted Argentina against France in a contest of remarkable swings. Lionel Messi converted a penalty in the 23rd minute and Angel Di Maria added a second in the 36th, before Kylian Mbappe struck twice in quick succession, a penalty in the 80th minute and another goal in the 81st, to force extra time at 2-2. Messi restored Argentina's lead in the 108th minute, only for Mbappe to complete his hat-trick from the penalty spot in the 118th, making it 3-3. Argentina prevailed 4-2 on penalties. Mbappe became only the second man to score a hat-trick in a World Cup final after Geoff Hurst in 1966, yet finished on the losing side, while also claiming the Golden Boot as top scorer with eight goals. Messi won the Golden Ball, becoming the first player to take the award twice after his 2014 honour, lifting the trophy as the crowning achievement of his career and securing Argentina's third title, after 1978 and 1986.
